title: Waveland, MS | CRS Activity 510
text:
CRS Planning Support
This project supported the City of Waveland in developing an Activity 510 floodplain management plan, substantial damage management plan, and repetitive loss area analysis for FEMA’s Community Rating System.
The project combined spatial flood risk analysis, NFIP policy and claims data, and community vulnerability indicators to identify areas of greatest concern and inform local floodplain management priorities.



Project Work

Flood hazard and exposure mapping
NFIP policy and claims analysis
Floodplain management planning and plan development

Data
OpenFEMA NFIP • County parcel data • NOAA sea level rise • SLOSH storm surge • MDEQ digital elevation model • USGS Shorelines • HUC watersheds
Methods


View R code
#load packages
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, duckdb, tigris)

#connect to the database 
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# query data for your area of interest (i.e., update the county code for your FIPs)
nfip_policy_raw <- dbGetQuery(con, "
                   SELECT *
                   FROM read_csv_auto('data/FimaNfipPoliciesV2.csv')
                   WHERE countyCode = 01097
                   ") 

# make variables with different resident types (optional)
single_family <- c(1, 11, 14)
two_to_four_family = c(2, 12)
multi_family <- c(3, 13, 15, 16)
non_residential <- c(4, 6, 17, 18, 19)

#set end date
end_date <- as.Date("2026-01-17") 

# tidy the data and make new variables
nfip_policy <- 
  nfip_policy_raw %>%
  transmute(
    across(c(policyEffectiveDate,
             policyTerminationDate,
             cancellationDateOfFloodPolicy), ~ as.Date(.x)), 
    countyCode,
    nfipCommunityName,
    nfipRatedCommunityNumber,
    
    effective = ifelse( #indicates whether the policy is effective
      policyEffectiveDate <= end_date &
      policyTerminationDate >= end_date &
        (cancellationDateOfFloodPolicy >= end_date |
           is.na(cancellationDateOfFloodPolicy)), 1, 0
    ),
    
    #create residence type variables
    single_family = ifelse(occupancyType %in% single_family, 1, 0),
    two_to_four_family = ifelse(occupancyType %in% two_to_four_family, 1, 0),
    multi_family = ifelse(occupancyType %in% multi_family, 1, 0),
    non_residential = ifelse(occupancyType %in% non_residential, 1, 0),
    occupancy_type = case_when(
      single_family == 1 ~ "Single Family",
      two_to_four_family == 1 ~ "2-4 Family",
      multi_family == 1 ~ "All Other Residential",
      non_residential == 1 ~ "Non-Residential"
    ) %>%
      factor(levels = c("Single Family", "2-4 Family", 
                        "All Other Residential", "Non-Residential")),
    
    #coverage amount variables
    totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy,
    totalBuildingInsuranceCoverage,
    totalContentsInsuranceCoverage,
    total_coverage = 
      totalBuildingInsuranceCoverage + 
      totalContentsInsuranceCoverage
  ) %>%
  filter(
    effective == 1 &
    countyCode == "01097" &
    nfipRatedCommunityNumber == "220139" #need to update !
    )

# create a table broken apart by residence type
nfip_policy %>%
  group_by(occupancy_type) %>% 
  summarize(
    number_policies = n(),
    total_premium = sum(totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy), 
    insurance_in_force = sum(total_coverage),
    .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      occupancy_type = "Total",
      number_policies = nrow(nfip_policy),
      total_premium = sum(nfip_policy$totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy), 
      insurance_in_force = sum(nfip_policy$total_coverage)
      )
    ) %>%
  transmute(
    'Occupancy Type' = occupancy_type,
    'Number of Policies in Force' = comma(number_policies),
    'Total Premium' = comma(total_premium),
    'Insurance in Force' = comma(insurance_in_force)
    )

title: Mapping Flood Insurance Participation
text:
In this project, I used OpenFEMA data to map the distribution of National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) coverage and identify areas with relatively low levels of participation.
The map below presents two measures of policy participation: the total number of effective residential NFIP policies and residential policies normalized by the number of housing units. Mapping both measures distinguishes places with large numbers of policies simply because they contain more households from places where flood insurance is more prevalent relative to the local housing stock.






Data & Methods: OpenFEMA NFIP Policies · U.S. Census/ACS housing data · R · sf · leaflet · rfema
All code used to extract OpenFEMA NFIP policy data and American Community Survey estimates, process the data, and create this map is available on GitHub here.

title: D’Iberville, MS | CRS Activity 610
text:
CRS Planning Support
This project was completed using funding allocated by the Mississippi Department of Marine Resources to support coastal communities in pursuing Community Rating System (CRS) credit.
From October 2025 to present (August 2026), I have supported resilience planners in the development of Community Rating System (CRS) Activity 610 flood response plans, contributing to both the planning process and the technical analysis required to support CRS crediting.
My work included participating in stakeholder meetings, contributing to plan writing, and compiling and analyzing flood-risk and community data. I also supported communities in selecting appropriate coastal and riverine flood scenarios, using SLOSH storm surge modeling and NOAA riverine flood inundation data to evaluate potential flood conditions and inform response planning.
A major component of my work involved spatial analysis of buildings covered by each flood response plan, identifying structures within the selected flood scenarios and supporting the calculation of CRS credit adjustments. I developed maps and other GIS-based analyses to communicate flood extent, document plan coverage, and support the planning and CRS documentation process.

As a Coastal Mississippi Resilience Fellow, I analyze and visualize a wide variety of data types, including demographic, land use, hazard, and insurance-related datasets, to support planning and decision making. I have supported municipal planning, community engagement, project implementation, and have helped secure over $6 million in state, regional, and federal grant funds for communities across southern Mississippi.
Before my fellowship, I worked as a research assistant on an NSF funded project, where I integrated structure-level datasets created by scientists with the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and The Water Institute into a comprehensive hierarchical geospatial dataset covering nearly 1 million structures in southern Louisiana.
In August 2026, I graduated with my Ph.D. in sociology, where my research focused on inequities in flooding and disaster recovery, particularly for flood impacts that are attributable to climate change. Before this, I graduated with a M.S. from the University of North Texas in 2022 and B.S. from Texas A&M University in 2020.

title: Climate Change & Federal Aid Dispersements
text:
Climate Change & Post-Harvey Federal Aid
In this project, I conducted a spatial analysis examining the relationship between climate change attributable flood damages and federal disaster assistance at the census tract level. The study area was Harris County, TX following Hurricane Harvey (2017).
I integrated modeled flood damages with census tract-level National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) and FEMA Individual Assistance (IA) disbursement data. Using climate attribution estimates from peer-reviewed research, the analysis compared damages under scenarios in which climate change increased Harvey’s rainfall by 20% and 38%. I applied spatial lag regression models to estimate both direct and spatial spillover relationships between attributable damages and federal recovery expenditures.
The results showed that while both attributable and non-attributable flood damages were associated with federal aid, climate change attributable damages generally had larger effect sizes, particularly for Individual Assistance.
The research highlights an important fiscal dimension of climate change: as climate change intensifies disaster damages, it can also increase the financial burden of recovery borne by federal programs and insurers.

title: Hurrican Ida: Wind & Storm Surge Attribution Analysis
text:
This interdisciplinary project with LSU, the National Center for Atmospheric Research, and The Water Institute examined Hurricane Ida’s impacts under changing climate conditions. I integrated modeled wind and storm-surge damage estimates with demographic data to analyze the distribution of climate-attributable impacts across communities.
